title: Material properties: strength, hardness, toughness
goals: Say what strength, hardness, toughness, ductility and stiffness each mean, and how each is tested
Work out tensile strength and elongation from a tensile test
Read a steel grade's toughness letters (JR, J0, J2) and say why cold matters
Compare steel, aluminium and titanium on strength, stiffness and weight
summary:
Different properties answer different questions. A file is very **hard** but snaps if dropped: hard, not **tough**.

- **Strength**: the stress it takes. **Yield strength**: where it starts to stay bent. **Ultimate tensile strength** (UTS): the most it takes. In MPa (N/mm²). Tested by pulling a bar in a **tensile test**: UTS = peak load ÷ original area.
- **Ductility**: how far it stretches before it breaks: **elongation** = increase in gauge length ÷ original × 100%. Ductile metals give warning; brittle ones (cast iron, glass, hardened tool steel) do not.
- **Hardness**: resistance to dents and scratches. Pressed in with an indenter: **Brinell** (HB, a ball), **Vickers** (HV, a diamond pyramid), **Rockwell** (HRC on hardened steels). Harder usually means stronger and more wear-resistant, but less tough.
- **Toughness**: the energy it absorbs before breaking, with a crack or notch. The **Charpy** test swings a pendulum through a notched bar and measures the joules absorbed. Steels lose toughness when **cold**: the grade letters say at what temperature 27 J is guaranteed: **JR** at +20 °C, **J0** at 0 °C, **J2** at −20 °C (S355J2, for example).
- **Stiffness**: Young's modulus $E$: steel about 200 GPa, titanium about 114, aluminium about 70.
- **Density**: steel about 7850 kg/m³, titanium about 4430, aluminium about 2700.

Strong is not stiff, and hard is not tough. Aluminium alloys can match mild steel's strength at a third of the weight, but bend three times as far. Titanium is strong, fairly light and resists corrosion: costly, so used where it pays (aerospace, chemical plant).

bench.task: Look up the material certificate (mill cert) for a steel delivery or a fabricated part at work.

Find the yield strength, tensile strength and elongation

cards.q: A hardened steel file is very hard, yet it can snap if dropped on a concrete floor. Which property does it lack?
options: Toughness
Hardness
Stiffness
Density
cards.why: Hardness is resistance to dents and scratches; toughness is the energy it can absorb before breaking. Hardening steel raises hardness and lowers toughness: a file is the extreme.

cards.title: Strength and the tensile test
cards.body:
**Strength** is the stress a material takes, in MPa (N/mm²). It is measured by pulling a standard bar until it breaks, a **tensile test**:

- **Yield strength** ($R_e$, or $R_{p0.2}$ where there is no clear yield): where it begins to stretch for good.
- **Ultimate tensile strength** ($R_m$, UTS): the peak load ÷ the original area.

Design works below yield. S275 structural steel: yield 275 MPa, UTS about 410–560 MPa.
cards.more:
The tensile machine records load against stretch. At first the bar stretches a tiny amount, in proportion to the load, and would spring back. Then at the yield point it starts to stretch much more for little extra load. Then the load climbs to a peak (the UTS) as the metal hardens by being stretched, before a neck forms and it breaks.

Aluminium and many alloy steels have no sharp yield point, so the **0.2% proof stress** is used: the stress that leaves a 0.2% permanent stretch.

The S in S275 is structural steel, and 275 is the minimum yield strength in MPa (for thinner sections).

cards.q: A tensile test bar of {ar} mm² breaks after a peak load of {kn} kN. What is its tensile strength?
cards.why: Tensile strength is the peak load over the original area; N/mm² is MPa.
cards.hint: kN × 1000 for newtons, ÷ the area in mm².

cards.title: Ductility: stretch before breaking
cards.body:
**Ductility** is how far a material stretches before it breaks. From the tensile test, the **elongation**: fit the broken halves together and measure the gauge length.

$$A\% = \frac{L_u - L_0}{L_0} \times 100$$

Mild steel: about 20–25%. Cast iron: under 1%: **brittle**.

Ductility is a safety margin: a ductile part bends and gives warning; a brittle one breaks suddenly. It also decides whether a part can be bent, pressed or drawn into shape.
cards.more:
Mark two lines 50 mm apart on a test bar. After it breaks, push the pieces together and measure between the lines: say 61 mm. It stretched 11 mm, which is $11 \div 50 = 22\%$.

A chocolate bar from the fridge snaps cleanly: brittle. Warm toffee stretches into strings before it parts: ductile. Most structural steels behave like the toffee at room temperature, which is why overloaded steelwork sags and twists before it collapses.

cards.q: A tensile bar's gauge marks were {l0} mm apart. After the break, fitted together, they are {lu} mm apart. What is the elongation?
cards.why: The increase over the original length, as a percentage.

cards.title: Hardness: dents and wear
cards.body:
**Hardness** is resistance to being dented or scratched. A hard indenter is pressed in under a set load and the dent is measured:

- **Brinell** (HB): a hard ball; a big dent, good for castings and softer steels
- **Vickers** (HV): a diamond pyramid; any material, small dents
- **Rockwell** (HRC for hardened steels): reads the depth directly; quick

Harder usually means more **wear** resistance and higher strength, but less toughness. Hardness tests are quick and nearly non-destructive, so they check heat treatment.
cards.more:
Press your thumbnail into wood, then into a steel plate: the wood dents. Hardness tests do that with a measured load and a tiny precise indenter.

A mild steel might be about 130 HB; a hardened tool steel 60 HRC or more (around 700 HV). Bearings and gear teeth are hardened at the surface for wear while their core stays tougher.

For steels, hardness and tensile strength go roughly together, so a hardness reading on a finished part gives a fair idea of its strength without cutting out a test bar (conversion tables are in ISO 18265).

cards.q: Match each hardness test with its indenter.
pairs: A diamond cone, reading the depth
cards.why: Each test presses a known indenter in under a set load and measures the dent: its size (Brinell, Vickers) or depth (Rockwell).

cards.title: Toughness, and the cold
cards.body:
**Toughness** is the energy a material absorbs before it breaks, especially with a notch or crack in it. The **Charpy** test swings a pendulum through a notched bar and measures the joules it took.

Many steels are tough when warm and turn **brittle when cold**. So a steel grade's letters say at what temperature it is guaranteed 27 J:

- **JR**: +20 °C
- **J0**: 0 °C
- **J2**: −20 °C

Outdoor structures in a UK winter call for J0 or J2.
cards.more:
Toughness is about cracks. A tough material, notched, still stretches and absorbs energy at the notch tip; a brittle one lets the crack run straight through.

The Charpy pendulum is lifted to a set height and dropped through the bar. The higher it swings on afterwards, the less energy the bar took: a tough bar slows it a lot.

Test the same steel at falling temperatures and the energy drops sharply over a range: the **ductile-to-brittle transition**. Ships and bridges have broken in two in cold weather because their steel was past it. S355J2 means: structural, 355 MPa yield, 27 J guaranteed at −20 °C.

cards.q: What does the 'J2' in S355J2 tell you?
options: It is guaranteed 27 J in a Charpy test at −20 °C
It is the second grade of S355 by strength
It has a yield strength of 355 MPa at 2 °C
It may be welded only with J2 electrodes
cards.why: The letters after the strength give the impact toughness: 27 J (J) at −20 °C (2). JR is at +20 °C and J0 at 0 °C. The 355 is the minimum yield strength in MPa.

cards.title: Stiffness and weight
cards.body:
**Stiffness** is Young's modulus, $E$: how much it bends under load, not how much it takes. **Density** is how heavy it is for its size.

- Steel: E about 200 GPa, density about 7850 kg/m³
- Titanium alloy: about 114 GPa, 4430 kg/m³
- Aluminium alloy: about 70 GPa, 2700 kg/m³

A strong aluminium alloy can match mild steel's strength at a third of the weight, but it bends three times as far. Strength per weight is what aircraft and moving machine parts care about.
cards.more:
Two beams of the same shape, one steel, one aluminium, the same load: the aluminium one sags three times as much, because E is a third. To match the steel's stiffness the aluminium section is made deeper, which is why aluminium extrusions are often bigger and boxier.

Per kilogram, though, aluminium does well: a third of the density, so a deeper section can still be lighter. For a gantry axis that accelerates hard, lighter moving parts mean a smaller motor.

Titanium sits between: much stronger than most aluminium, about half steel's stiffness, 57% of its weight, and very corrosion resistant.

cards.q: A steel bracket is swapped for an aluminium one of the same shape and the same strength. What changes most?
options: It deflects about three times as much
It breaks at about a third of the load
It weighs about three times as much
Nothing changes: the strength is the same
cards.why: Same strength, so it takes the same load before yielding. But aluminium's E is about a third of steel's, so it bends about three times as far. It also weighs about a third as much.

cards.q: Match each property with what it means.
pairs: The stress it takes before yielding or breaking
How well it resists dents and scratches
The energy it absorbs before it fractures
How far it stretches before it breaks
How little it bends under load
cards.why: Five different questions about a material, with five different tests.

cards.q: Match each test with what it measures.
A round test bar {dd} mm in diameter breaks at {kn} kN. What is its tensile strength?
cards.why: Area of the round bar first, then the peak load over it.

cards.q: A crane runway outdoors in Scotland is to be made of S355. Why might the designer ask for S355J2 rather than S355JR?
options: J2 is tested tough at −20 °C; JR only at +20 °C
J2 has a higher yield strength than JR
J2 is easier to cut and drill than JR
JR cannot be used outdoors at all
cards.why: Steel can turn brittle in the cold. JR only guarantees toughness at room temperature; J2 guarantees it at −20 °C, which a Scottish winter can reach. Both have the same 355 MPa yield.

cards.back: Steel about 7850 kg/m³; titanium about 4430; aluminium about 2700.
Steel about 200 GPa; titanium alloy about 114 GPa; aluminium about 70 GPa.

cards.q: Gear teeth are often case hardened: hard at the surface, softer in the middle. Why?
options: Hard skin for wear, tough core against snapping
It makes the gear lighter overall
A soft core makes the gear stiffer
So the teeth can be machined afterwards
cards.why: Hardness resists wear where the teeth rub; a tougher core absorbs shock loads without the tooth snapping. Through-hardening would make the whole tooth brittle.

cards.q: A glass rod is hard and strong in compression, but shatters when struck. Which property is it short of?
options: Toughness
Hardness
Stiffness
Strength in compression
cards.why: Glass is hard and stiff but absorbs very little energy before cracking: it is brittle, with low toughness.
